content: 1. The treatment regimen for extensively drug-resistant tuberculosis (XDR-TB) should be individualized for each patient. A standardized regimen may only be used under operational research conditions, which require ethical approval, patient-centered care and support, predefined eligibility criteria, informed consent, adherence to good clinical practice, active drug safety monitoring (aDSM), treatment monitoring, outcome evaluation, and comprehensive, standardized data collection. 2. When using a fixed-dose combination of rifampicin, ethambutol, and pyrazinamide (REZ), isoniazid (H) may be added. If levofloxacin (Lfx) cannot be used, the remaining treatment regimen can still be prescribed. 3. A shorter treatment regimen for multidrug-resistant or rifampin-resistant tuberculosis (MDR/RR-TB) consists of all-oral TB drugs and must include bedaquiline (Bdq). This regimen is recommended for patients who meet the following criteria: (i) laboratory-confirmed MDR/RR-TB, (ii) no prior exposure to second-line TB drugs in this regimen (or exposure for less than one month), and (iii) no evidence of resistance to fluoroquinolones. 4. The shorter MDR/RR-TB regimen is typically four months long but may be extended to six months if the patient remains sputum smear-positive or culture-positive at the end of the fourth month. Bedaquiline is used for six months in this regimen. 5. The longer MDR/RR-TB regimen is prescribed for patients who are not eligible for the shorter regimen. It should be tailored to each patient, ensuring the use of at least four effective drugs during the first six months of intensive treatment and three effective drugs during the continuation phase, which lasts 12 months or more. Group C drugs may be added to replace ineffective Group A and Group B drugs. 6. A new four-month treatment regimen for drug-susceptible tuberculosis, consisting of rifapentine, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and moxifloxacin, has shown similar efficacy and safety compared to the current standard regimen. This shorter, all-oral regimen is preferred for many patients and national TB programs (NTPs) as it allows faster cure, reduces the burden on patients and healthcare systems, improves adherence, and lowers costs. 7. Patient-centered TB care is tailored to individual values and needs, aiming to address all health requirements. It involves a partnership between patients and caregivers to choose the most convenient treatment methods. This includes health education, counseling for disease and treatment adherence, and a package of adherence interventions based on patient needs, provider resources, and implementation conditions. 8. Treatment administration options, in order of preference, include: (a) directly observed treatment (DOT) by trained lay providers or healthcare workers at the community level, (b) video-observed treatment (VOT) if supporting technology is available, (c) DOT by healthcare workers at health facilities, (d) DOT by family members, and (e) unsupervised treatment. 9. Adverse drug effects are categorized as minor (not requiring treatment interruption) or major (requiring treatment interruption). Examples of minor effects include anorexia, nausea, abdominal pain, drowsiness, metallic taste, and joint pain. Major effects include severe anorexia, peripheral neuropathy, skin rash, vestibular toxicity, visual impairment, hematological abnormalities, QT prolongation, and hepatitis. Each adverse effect is associated with specific suspected drugs and requires appropriate levels of care. 10. Preventive treatment for drug-susceptible TB infection includes several recommended regimens based on the epidemiological context. Options include six months of isoniazid (6H), three to four months of rifampicin (3-4R), three months of isoniazid and rifampicin (3HR), or three months of isoniazid and rifapentine (3H7-Rpt7H). Dosages vary by age and weight, and some regimens may interfere with antiretroviral drugs. 11. Preventive treatment for latent drug-resistant TB infection should be carefully considered based on exposure intensity, source case certainty, drug resistance patterns, and potential adverse events. Treatment should be prescribed by a specialist and limited to high-risk household contacts, such as children, immunosuppressed individuals, and people living with HIV. Latent infection must be confirmed before treatment, and patients should be closely monitored for adverse events, adherence, and the development of active TB disease for at least two years. Treatment regimens should be chosen based on reliable information about the source case's drug resistance profile.
